title: Error Handling
summary: **Error handling** is how JavaScript detects, reports, and recovers from failures. The core tools are `throw` to raise an error, `try/catch/finally` to handle it, and the `Error` object that carries a message and stack — extended by custom error types and async-aware patterns for promises.

subtopics.title: try/catch/finally
subtopics.explanation: Wrap risky code in `try`; if anything throws, control jumps to `catch` with the error. `finally` runs regardless of success or failure — ideal for cleanup like closing connections or hiding a loading spinner. Code after a thrown-and-caught error continues normally.
subtopics.example: try { risky(); } catch (e) { console.error(e); } finally { cleanup(); }

subtopics.title: throw
subtopics.explanation: `throw` raises an error and immediately stops the current execution, unwinding the call stack until a catch handles it (or the program crashes). You can throw any value, but you should throw an Error instance so consumers get a message and a stack trace.
subtopics.example: if (n < 0) throw new Error('n must be non-negative');

subtopics.title: The Error object and built-in types
subtopics.explanation: An Error carries a `name`, a `message`, and a `stack`. JavaScript has built-in subtypes: TypeError (wrong type/calling non-functions), RangeError (out of range), SyntaxError, ReferenceError (undeclared variable), and more. Checking the error's type lets you respond appropriately.

subtopics.title: Custom error classes
subtopics.explanation: Extend the built-in Error to create domain-specific errors like ValidationError or NotFoundError. A custom class lets callers use `instanceof` to handle different failures differently, and you can attach extra fields (like a status code) for richer handling.
subtopics.example: class ValidationError extends Error { constructor(m){ super(m); this.name = 'ValidationError'; } }

subtopics.title: Errors in async code
subtopics.explanation: Inside async functions, a rejected awaited promise throws, so ordinary try/catch works. But errors thrown asynchronously (e.g. inside a setTimeout callback) escape the surrounding try/catch because that callback runs later, on its own stack — handle those where they actually run.
subtopics.example: async function f(){ try { await mayReject(); } catch (e) { handle(e); } }

subtopics.title: Rejected promises
subtopics.explanation: A rejected promise is the async equivalent of a thrown error. Handle it with `.catch()` or with try/catch around `await`. An unhandled rejection triggers an 'unhandledrejection' event and can crash Node or log warnings — never leave a promise's rejection unhandled.

subtopics.title: Error-first callbacks
subtopics.explanation: Before promises, Node used the error-first convention: callbacks receive `(err, data)`, where a truthy `err` signals failure. You must check `err` first and return early; forgetting to handle it is a classic bug that lets failures pass silently.
subtopics.example: fs.readFile(path, (err, data) => { if (err) return handle(err); use(data); });

subtopics.title: Graceful degradation
subtopics.explanation: Good error handling doesn't just log — it keeps the app usable. Provide fallbacks (cached data, default values, a friendly message) so one failing feature doesn't break the whole page. Catch errors at boundaries and show a recoverable state instead of a blank screen.
subtopics.example: try { return JSON.parse(raw); } catch { return defaultConfig; }

subtopics.title: Rethrowing
subtopics.explanation: Sometimes a catch block can't fully handle an error — it should log or add context, then rethrow so a higher-level handler can decide. Swallowing errors silently (an empty catch) hides bugs; rethrow (optionally wrapping in a richer error) to preserve the failure.
subtopics.example: catch (e) { logger.error(e); throw e; } // let caller handle it too

foundations.overview: Error handling in JavaScript revolves around throwing and catching errors. Synchronous failures use throw + try/catch/finally; asynchronous failures use rejected promises handled by .catch() or try/catch around await. The Error object standardizes failure information, and custom error classes plus instanceof let you route different failures to different recovery paths.
foundations.formalDefinition: An exception is a thrown value that interrupts normal control flow and propagates up the call stack until caught by a try/catch. In async code, the equivalent is a rejected Promise, whose rejection reason propagates through the promise chain until handled.
foundations.whyItMatters: Software fails — networks drop, inputs are invalid, APIs return errors. Handling these gracefully is the difference between a resilient app and one that crashes or silently corrupts data. It's also a core interview topic that reveals how carefully someone reasons about failure paths.
foundations.mentalModel: Think of try/catch as a safety net under a tightrope: code walks the rope, and if it falls (throws), the net (catch) catches it so the show goes on. finally is the crew that cleans up the stage whether the walk succeeded or not.
foundations.browserPerspective: Uncaught synchronous errors fire a window 'error' event and stop the current task; unhandled promise rejections fire 'unhandledrejection'. The engine unwinds the stack to find the nearest catch, building the stack trace as it goes.
foundations.realWorldUsage: Validating form input, guarding network calls, parsing JSON safely, wrapping third-party code, React error boundaries, and centralized logging all depend on deliberate error handling.
foundations.businessImpact: Graceful error handling reduces crashes, data loss, and support tickets, and lets users recover from failures instead of abandoning the app — directly protecting revenue and trust.
foundations.engineeringImpact: Consistent error types and boundaries make failures debuggable and testable, prevent silent corruption from swallowed errors, and clarify which layer owns each failure.
foundations.performanceImpact: throw/catch is cheap on the happy path; the cost comes from using exceptions for normal control flow or catching in tight loops. Errors should signal exceptional conditions, not routine branching.
commonUseCases: Validating inputs and throwing typed errors (ValidationError)
Guarding network/JSON operations with try/catch and fallbacks
Centralized logging plus rethrowing to preserve failures
Handling rejected promises with .catch() or try/catch around await

commonMisconceptions.myth: A try/catch around code that uses setTimeout catches errors thrown inside the timeout callback.
commonMisconceptions.reality: The callback runs later on its own stack, so the surrounding try/catch is long gone — handle the error inside the callback.

commonMisconceptions.myth: An empty catch block is fine if you don't care about the error.
commonMisconceptions.reality: Swallowing errors hides bugs and makes failures invisible; at minimum log, and usually rethrow or handle meaningfully.

config.intro: Follow an error from the throw point up to the handler that catches it.

steps.name: Enter try block
steps.detail: Code runs normally until a statement throws an error.

steps.name: throw fires
steps.detail: Execution stops at the throw and an Error object (with message + stack) is created.

steps.name: Stack unwinds
steps.detail: The engine walks up the call stack looking for the nearest enclosing catch.

steps.name: catch handles it
steps.detail: Control jumps to the catch block, which receives the error and can recover or rethrow.

steps.name: finally runs
steps.detail: Cleanup in finally executes whether or not an error occurred.

steps.name: Resume or crash
steps.detail: If caught, code after the try/catch continues; if uncaught, it reaches the global handler.

debuggingLab.title: try/catch that misses async errors
debuggingLab.symptom: The error thrown inside the timeout escapes the try/catch and shows as an uncaught error instead of being handled.
debuggingLab.errorAnalysis: The try/catch only wraps the call that schedules the timeout, which returns immediately. The callback runs later on a fresh stack, long after the try/catch has exited, so the throw is uncaught.
commonMistakes: Assuming a try/catch covers errors thrown in async callbacks scheduled inside it.
Mixing callback-based timers with synchronous error handling expectations.
debuggingLab.fixChallenge: Move the error handling to where the async code actually runs (inside the callback), or convert to a promise and await it inside try/catch.

theory.question: Explain try/catch/finally and what each part does.
theory.directAnswer: `try` holds code that might throw. If it throws, control jumps to `catch`, which receives the error and can recover, log, or rethrow. `finally` runs afterward no matter what — success, caught error, or even a return — making it ideal for cleanup like closing resources or hiding a loading state.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: A control-flow construct for catching exceptions and guaranteeing cleanup.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: To separate the happy path from failure handling and ensure resources are released regardless of outcome.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: A throw inside try unwinds to the catch; finally executes on every exit path from the try/catch.

theory.whyImportant: It's the foundation of synchronous error handling and is asked in nearly every JS interview.
theory.realWorldExample: Showing a spinner in try, parsing a response, and hiding the spinner in finally so it always disappears.

nestedTopics.title: finally always runs
nestedTopics.explanation: Executes even if try returns or catch rethrows.

nestedTopics.title: Catching the error
nestedTopics.explanation: catch (e) binds the thrown value for inspection.

nestedTopics.title: Optional catch binding
nestedTopics.explanation: You can write catch { } when you don't need the error object.

followUps.question: Does finally run if try returns a value?
followUps.answer: Yes — finally runs before the function actually returns, which is why it's used for cleanup.

followUps.question: Can you have try/finally without catch?
followUps.answer: Yes — to guarantee cleanup while letting the error propagate to a higher handler.

theory.question: What is the Error object, what built-in error types exist, and why create custom errors?
theory.directAnswer: An Error has a name, message, and stack. Built-in subtypes include TypeError, RangeError, ReferenceError, and SyntaxError, each signaling a specific failure category. Custom error classes (extending Error) let you model domain failures like ValidationError, use instanceof to route handling, and attach extra fields such as a status code.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Error is the base type for thrown failures; subclasses specialize it.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Standardizing failure info (message + stack) makes errors debuggable and lets handlers branch on type.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Extend Error, call super(message), set this.name, and optionally add properties; consumers check instanceof.

theory.whyImportant: Typed errors enable precise recovery (e.g., show a form message for ValidationError, retry for NetworkError) and are common in interviews.
theory.realWorldExample: An API client throws a NotFoundError with a status field so the UI can show a 404 page.

nestedTopics.title: instanceof checks
nestedTopics.explanation: Distinguish custom error types in catch to choose recovery.

nestedTopics.title: Stack traces
nestedTopics.explanation: error.stack records where the error originated for debugging.

followUps.question: Why throw an Error instead of a string?
followUps.answer: Errors carry a stack trace and a consistent shape; throwing a string loses that and breaks tooling and instanceof checks.

scenario.question: A page goes completely blank whenever one API call fails. How would you make it degrade gracefully instead?
scenario.directAnswer: I'd catch the failure at a boundary rather than letting it propagate to a crash. Wrap the call in try/catch (or .catch()), log the error, and render a fallback — cached data, a default value, or a friendly 'couldn't load' message with a retry — so the rest of the page stays functional.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Graceful degradation: containing failures so one broken feature doesn't take down the whole UI.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Uncaught errors bubble up and can break rendering entirely; boundaries scope the blast radius.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Catch at the feature/component boundary, log for observability, and substitute a recoverable fallback state.

scenario.whyImportant: Resilience to partial failure is a hallmark of production-quality frontends and a common design discussion.

nestedTopics.title: Error boundaries
nestedTopics.explanation: In React, components that catch render errors and show fallback UI.

nestedTopics.title: Fallback values
nestedTopics.explanation: Defaults or cached data keep the feature usable when fresh data fails.

followUps.question: Where should you NOT swallow the error?
followUps.answer: Don't swallow silently — always log (and often report to monitoring) so the failure is visible even though the UI recovers.

coding.question: Implement a tryCatch(fn) wrapper for async functions that returns a [error, data] tuple instead of throwing.
coding.thoughtProcess: Go-style error handling avoids try/catch at every call site. I'll write an async helper that awaits fn(): on success it returns [null, data]; on failure it catches and returns [error, undefined]. Callers then check the first element.
coding.lineByLine: We await fn() inside try. On success we return [null, data] so the error slot is empty. If fn rejects or throws, the catch returns [error, undefined]. The caller destructures the tuple and branches on err, keeping call sites flat and explicit.

alternativeApproaches.title: Plain try/catch at call site
alternativeApproaches.explanation: Simpler but adds a try/catch block around every async call, which gets verbose.
alternativeApproaches.code: try { const u = await getUser(1); } catch (e) {}

followUps.question: What's a downside of the tuple pattern?
followUps.answer: It's easy to forget to check the error element, and it can obscure stack traces compared to letting the error propagate to a dedicated handler.

productionDeepDive.architecture: Production systems handle errors at boundaries: input validation throws typed errors, service calls catch and normalize failures, and a top-level handler (or React error boundary) renders fallback UI and reports to monitoring. Errors carry consistent shapes for predictable handling.
productionDeepDive.performance: Exceptions are fine for exceptional cases but should not drive normal control flow or fire in hot loops. Keep the happy path free of try/catch where validation can prevent the error instead.
productionDeepDive.security: Never leak internal details (stack traces, SQL, paths) to end users; log them server-side and show generic messages. Sanitize error messages rendered in the UI to avoid injection, and fail closed on auth errors.
productionDeepDive.scaling: Add retries with backoff for transient failures, circuit breakers for failing dependencies, and rate-limit-aware handling so error storms don't cascade across services.
productionDeepDive.maintainability: Custom error classes and centralized handlers make failures self-documenting and testable; banning empty catch blocks (via lint rules) prevents silent bug-hiding.
productionDeepDive.observability: Capture both synchronous errors and unhandled promise rejections globally (window 'error'/'unhandledrejection' or process handlers), attach context, and send to an error-tracking service like Sentry.

caseStudies.problem: A single uncaught error blanked the whole app.
caseStudies.solution: Introduced error boundaries plus per-feature try/catch with fallback UI and monitoring.
caseStudies.tradeoffs: More handling code and fallback states to maintain.
caseStudies.lessons: Containing failures at boundaries turns total crashes into recoverable, observable incidents.

keyTakeaways: Use throw to raise errors and try/catch/finally to handle them; finally always runs for cleanup.
Throw Error instances (or subclasses) so failures carry a message and stack, and use instanceof to route handling.
Async failures are rejected promises — handle them with .catch() or try/catch around await, and never leave rejections unhandled.
A try/catch does NOT catch errors thrown later in async callbacks like setTimeout; handle them where they run.
Degrade gracefully: log, provide fallbacks, and rethrow rather than swallowing errors silently.
